text: In one screen A reranker is a second, slower and more accurate model that re-orders the short list a first retriever returns.
label: core
key: re-orders the first stage's top k

text: The first stage (BM25 or a vector search, often both) looks at the whole corpus and keeps the top K candidates, say 30 out of 5,183 abstracts; the reranker reads each candidate together with the query and gives it a new score; the top few go to the language model.
label: core

text: The idea is old (search engines have used two-stage ranking for decades) and the reason is cost: a model that reads query and document together cannot precompute anything, so it can afford to look at only a few candidates per query. corpus (5,183 abstracts) → first stage: BM25, vectors, hybrid → top K (10 to 100) → reranker : score each (query, candidate) → top k (3 to 10) → LLM Six ideas that carry the page 1.
label: core

text: Cost per pair, not per query A vector search pays one model pass per query; a reranker pays one per candidate.
label: fat

text: Measured here, reranking all 5,183 abstracts for one claim would take 22 s with the 22 M MiniLM cross-encoder and 17 minutes with Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B.
label: core

text: That is why K is small (sections 1 and 4).
label: core
key: that is why k is small

text: A reranker only helps if it is stronger On SciFact the small MiniLM cross-encoder lifts BM25 (0.679 to 0.688) but lowers the hybrid list (0.724 to 0.689 at K = 100), while Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B lifts it to 0.783 (section 4).
label: core

text: Depth has a ceiling and a sweet spot A reranker cannot surface what the first stage did not return: recall@K of the hybrid list is 0.862 at K = 10 and 0.921 at K = 30.
label: core

text: Past about K = 20 to 30 quality stops rising here while cost keeps rising linearly (section 4, Depth chooser tab).
label: fat

text: Scores are not probabilities The three rerankers here return three different things (a raw logit, a sigmoid, a yes-minus-no log-odds).
label: core

text: Thresholds do not transfer between models or domains, but a reranker's top score is a better "nothing relevant here" signal than the retriever's: AUROC 0.80 against 0.72 for the cosine (section 5).

text: Why a second stage The problem.
label: fat

text: A first-stage retriever must look at every document for every query, so it can only afford a cheap comparison.
label: core
key: can only afford a cheap comparison

text: A bi-encoder (the usual "embedding model") encodes the query and each document separately into one vector each; documents are encoded once, offline, and a query costs one model pass plus N dot products.
label: core

text: Encoding separately is also its weakness: the document vector was fixed before the query existed, so it has to summarise everything the document might be asked about in about a thousand numbers.
label: core

text: BM25 is cheaper still and only counts shared words.
label: core

text: How a reranker fixes it.
label: fat

text: A cross-encoder puts the query and one document into the same transformer input, so every query token can attend to every document token in every layer, and the model outputs one relevance score for that pair.
label: core
key: every query token attends to every document token

text: It sees "MDA5" in the claim next to "RIG-I, MDA5, and LGP2" in the abstract, rather than two summaries of them.
label: core

text: Nothing can be precomputed, so it is run only on the first stage's top K.
label: core
key: runs only on the top k

text: Cross-encoders, read in the code The architecture.
label: fat

text: A BERT-style cross-encoder takes one sequence, [CLS] query [SEP] document [SEP] , with a segment id of 0 on the query part and 1 on the document part, runs it through the encoder (6 layers for MiniLM-L6, 24 for bge-reranker-v2-m3), takes the final vector of the [CLS] token, and maps it to one number with a small head.
label: core

text: That number is the relevance logit (an unbounded score; higher means more relevant).
label: core

text: This is exactly the 2019 recipe of Nogueira and Cho : "we feed the query as sentence A and the passage text as sentence B", the query cut to 64 tokens and the pair to 512, and "the [CLS] vector as input to a single layer neural network".
label: core

text: They reranked BM25's top 1,000 on MS MARCO and moved MRR@10 on the dev set from 16.7 (BM25) to 36.5 (BERT Large) (Table 1; published, independent academic , 2019).

text: How cross-encoders are trained The data.
label: fat

text: Almost every open English reranker starts from MS MARCO passage ranking: 8,841,823 passages from Bing results and 1,010,916 anonymised questions ( Bajaj et al., v3 ), with 532,761 training relevance labels and official training triples (query, positive, negative): 39,780,811 in the small file ( dataset page , read 2026-10-14).
label: depth

text: Labels are sparse: usually one marked passage per question, so many "negatives" are relevant passages nobody marked ( false negatives ).
label: core

text: Three losses, in the order they appeared.
label: core

text: Pointwise : binary cross-entropy on each (query, passage, label), as Nogueira and Cho did: the model learns "is this passage relevant", one pair at a time.
label: core

text: Hard negatives : negatives taken from a retriever's top results (BM25's top 1,000 in 2019, a dense retriever's later) rather than at random.
label: depth

text: A random abstract about cardiology is trivially irrelevant to a claim about MDA5; the abstract about RIG-I signalling that mentions MDA5 but does not support the claim is what the model must learn to rank second.
label: core

text: Distillation (section 7): the student learns a stronger teacher's scores instead of 0/1 labels.
label: core

text: The sentence-transformers MS MARCO cross-encoders were trained this way: "we use knowledge distillation with a small & fast model and learn the logits scores from the teacher ensemble" (BERT-base, BERT-large, ALBERT-large, from Hofstätter et al., 2020 ); the training script's loss is a pointwise mean squared error on the ensemble's logits ( examples/training/ms_marco/train_cross-encoder_kd.py in sentence-transformers v2.2.2).
label: depth

text: The model card itself only says it "was trained on the MS Marco Passage Ranking task", so which script produced the released checkpoint is not stated: unconfirmed.
label: depth

text: The model card's own table ( published, vendor , read 2026-10-14) shows the size trade: MiniLM-L6-v2 74.30 nDCG@10 on TREC DL 2019 and 39.01 MRR@10 on MS MARCO dev at 1,800 documents/s on a V100, against 74.31 and 39.02 at 960 documents/s for the 12-layer version: half the layers cost nothing measurable there.
label: depth

text: Its chat template (shipped with the model, chat_template.jinja ) puts the task in a fixed frame and pre-fills an empty thinking block, so the very next token must be the answer: <|im_start|>system Judge whether the Document meets the requirements based on the Query and the Instruct provided.

text: Note that the answer can only be "yes" or "no".<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user <Instruct>: {{ instruction }} <Query>: {{ query_text }} <Document>: {{ document_text }}<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant <think> </think> sentence-transformers 6.1.0, cross_encoder/modules/logit_score.py , lines 42-54 (abridged) def forward(self, features, **kwargs): logits = features[self.module_input_name][:, -1] # next-token logits at the last position if self.false_token_id is None: scores = logits[:, self.true_token_id] else: scores = logits[:, self.true_token_id] - logits[:, self.false_token_id] # "yes" (9693) minus "no" (2152) features["scores"] = scores.unsqueeze(1) Why the difference of two logits: a softmax restricted to the two tokens gives P(yes) = e y / (e y + e n ) = sigmoid(y - n), so the stored score is the log-odds of "yes" against "no", and sigmoid(score) is that probability.
label: depth

text: Late interaction: ColBERT and MaxSim The idea.
label: fat

text: A bi-encoder squeezes a document into one vector; a cross-encoder reads query and document together and precomputes nothing.
label: core

text: Late interaction keeps the document side precomputable but much richer: the encoder outputs one small vector per token , stored offline, and the query and document only "interact" at the end, through a cheap score.
label: core

text: ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020) defines that score as MaxSim : for each query token, take its highest dot product with any document token, then add those maxima up. score(q, d) = ∑ i ∈ query tokens max j ∈ document tokens q i · d j Each query token looks for its own best match: "md ##a ##5" in claim 1180 finds the same three word pieces in the abstract (similarities 0.96, 0.97 and 0.96), "sensor" finds "sensing" (0.92), "rna", "virus" and "infection" find themselves.
label: core

text: Watch it token by token, against the single-vector cosine on the same pair, in the MaxSim lab tab. pylate 1.6.0, scores/colbert.py , lines 189-200 (the plain torch path) scores = torch.einsum("ash,bth->abst", queries_embeddings, documents_embeddings) # every query token x every doc token if queries_mask is not None: scores = scores * queries_mask.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(3) if documents_mask is not None: scores = scores * documents_mask.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(2) scores = scores.max(axis=-1).values.sum(axis=-1) # max over doc tokens, sum over query tokens Three details that matter , all from the paper and visible in pylate's models/colbert.py : Markers.
label: depth

text: A query starts [CLS] [Q] , a document [CLS] [D] (here the unused vocabulary slots [unused0] and [unused1] ), so one encoder can embed both differently.
label: core

text: Queries are padded with [MASK] tokens to a fixed 32 (pylate sets the pad token to the mask token, lines 411-412, and pads queries to max_length , lines 1173-1178).
label: depth

text: The [MASK] vectors are kept and scored like real tokens: a learned soft query expansion.
label: core

text: SciFact claims have 22.7 real tokens on average, so about 29% of each query is [MASK].

text: PLAID: compressing and searching token vectors The problem.
label: fat

section: 9. plaid: compressing and searching token vectors
text: One vector per token multiplies storage by the number of tokens (236 here), and exhaustive MaxSim reads all of them.
label: core
key: multiplies storage by the tokens per document

section: 9. plaid: compressing and searching token vectors
text: ColBERTv2 compresses each token vector as the id of its nearest k-means centroid plus the residual (vector minus centroid) quantised to 1 or 2 bits per dimension: "this total of 20 or 36 bytes per vector" at 128 dimensions against 256 bytes in float16, a 6 to 10 times smaller index.
label: core

section: 9. plaid: compressing and searching token vectors
text: PLAID then searches without decompressing everything: (1) each query token picks its nearest centroids and the documents with tokens in them become candidates; (2) and (3) candidates are scored with centroid interaction , MaxSim with every token replaced by its centroid, pruning centroids that score low for every query token; (4) only the survivors are decompressed and scored exactly.
label: core

section: 9. plaid: compressing and searching token vectors
text: PLAID's Table 3 reports 39.8 MRR@10 on MS MARCO at k = 100 in 222 ms on one CPU core and 20 ms on a GPU, against 4,569 ms on 8 cores for vanilla ColBERTv2 ( published, academic, 2022 ).
